summary.text: Impulse is the change in an object's momentum, most often used for forces that act for a short time, as in impacts and collisions.
Like momentum it has a size and a direction, and its SI unit is the newton-second, dimensionally equal to kilogram metre per second.
A constant force acting for a time gives an impulse equal to force times time, and in rocketry impulse per unit of propellant gives a performance number called specific impulse.

paragraphs.heading: Change in momentum
paragraphs.text: Impulse is the change in an object's momentum, usually written J. If an object's momentum begins at pᵢ and ends at p_f, the impulse is J = p_f − pᵢ. It is mostly used for forces that act briefly, such as in impacts and collisions, which is where its name comes from.

paragraphs.heading: Size and direction
paragraphs.text: Impulse is a vector. Its size tells you how much the momentum changed, and its direction tells you which way. It shares the units and dimensions of momentum. In SI units it is measured in newton-seconds, N⋅s, which equal kilogram-metres per second.

paragraphs.heading: Force times time
paragraphs.text: Newton's second law says the net force on an object equals how fast its momentum changes. So a steady force F acting for a time Δt delivers an impulse J = FΔt.

paragraphs.heading: The instant-change model
paragraphs.text: For a very brief force, impulse is often treated as if the momentum jumped all at once. Such a sudden step change cannot really happen. Still, the shortcut is handy for working out ideal collisions, for example in videogame physics engines.

paragraphs.heading: Rockets and impulse
paragraphs.text: Impulse is a working tool for analysing jet and rocket vehicles, and in rocketry total impulse means the same thing as impulse. Dividing the impulse a rocket delivers by the mass of propellant it burns gives specific impulse, a measure of engine performance. Specific impulse feeds into the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, which links a vehicle's change in velocity to its engine's specific impulse and its propellant-mass ratio.

paragraphs.heading: When mass is lost
paragraphs.text: Newton's second law in the form F = dp/dt holds only when no mass flows into or out of the object. For an object whose mass changes, such as a rocket, you can instead treat the escaping material as a series of small masses. The specific impulse then turns out to be the exhaust velocity, the speed at which material leaves the rocket as seen from the rocket.
